This is the correct port to use for recharging your vehicle's air conditioning system.

Here are a few important details and safety checks before you attach your R1234YF Blaster kit:

System Verifications

  • Refrigerant Match: The factory sticker visible at the top edge of your photo explicitly states the system uses R-1234yf, which perfectly matches your recharge kit.
  • Port Safety Design: The low-pressure port is always located on the thicker pipe (the suction line). The quick-connect coupler on your recharge kit is intentionally sized to fit only this low-pressure port. If the fitting does not easily click into place, do not force it.

Connection Guidelines

  1. Prepare the Vehicle: Start the engine, turn the AC to the coldest temperature setting, and turn the fan to the highest speed. Ensure the compressor is engaging.
  2. Connect the Hose: Unscrew the grey cap, pull back the outer ring on the kit's quick-connect coupler, push it firmly down onto the port, and release the ring to lock it in place. Give it a gentle tug to ensure it is secure.
  3. Read the Gauge First: Before squeezing the trigger to dispense any refrigerant, read the pressure gauge on the kit. Only add refrigerant if the gauge indicates the pressure is low for the current ambient temperature. Overcharging the system can cause the compressor to fail or the AC to stop blowing cold air.

turns.prompt_text: It is 78 degrees F, I read 87 psi on the container guage
turns.response_html:
Gauge Reading Analysis

Do not pull the trigger to add refrigerant.

At 78°F, a normal, functioning low-side pressure while the AC is running should be sitting somewhere between 35 and 45 psi. A reading of 87 psi indicates that your system is currently at static pressure. This means the AC compressor is not engaging.

When the compressor is off, the high and low sides of the system equalize. The static pressure of R1234yf at roughly 78°F is right around 85–90 psi, which matches your reading perfectly.

Why This Happens and What to Do

Adding refrigerant while the compressor is off won't fix the issue and can dangerously overcharge the system, potentially causing a blowout or permanent compressor damage if it suddenly kicks on. Here are the immediate things to check:

  • Cabin Controls: Double-check that the vehicle is running, the AC is set to the absolute coldest setting, the fan is on its highest speed, and the recirculate button is on.
  • Electrical Faults: The compressor might be locked out due to a blown fuse or a faulty AC compressor relay.
  • Safety Switches: Even though you have static pressure (which means the system isn't completely empty), a faulty pressure sensor could be telling the vehicle's computer not to engage the clutch to protect the system.

Are you able to look down at the engine belt and see if the AC compressor clutch is spinning, or is the center of the pulley sitting completely still?

turns.prompt_text: Where is the AC compressor clutch belt located?
turns.response_html:
On your 2021 Chevy Malibu, the engine is mounted sideways (transverse). This means the serpentine belt—the main drive belt that runs the AC compressor—is located on the passenger side of the engine bay.

Here is how to locate it and check the clutch:

  1. Locate the Belt: Stand at the front bumper facing the engine bay. Look down to your left (the passenger side of the car). You will see a thick, grooved rubber belt winding around a series of pulleys.
  2. Find the Compressor: The AC compressor is a large, cylindrical metallic component. It is typically mounted lower down on that side of the engine, often directly below the alternator.
  3. Observe the Clutch: The compressor pulley has two main visual parts.
    • The outer ring (the pulley itself) will be spinning continuously because the engine is running and the belt is turning it.
    • The flat center plate inside that pulley is the clutch.
    • If that center plate is spinning in sync with the outer pulley, the compressor is actively engaged.
    • If the center plate is sitting completely still while the outer ring spins around it, the compressor is disengaged (which perfectly aligns with your 87 psi static pressure reading).

Safety Warning: Please be extremely careful when leaning over a running engine. Keep your hands, loose clothing, and tools well away from the spinning belt and radiator cooling fans.

If that center plate is definitely not spinning despite the AC controls being set to maximum cold inside the cabin, the vehicle's computer is locking out the compressor. Do you see it spinning, or is the center sitting still?

turns.prompt_text: The center plate is stationary
turns.response_html:
Diagnosis: Compressor Lockout

Since the center plate is stationary, your compressor is definitively disengaged. This perfectly explains the high reading of 87 psi on the low side—the system is sitting at normal static equalization for a 78°F ambient temperature.

Because your system is holding static pressure, a massive leak is likely not your primary issue right now. Instead, the vehicle's computer is intentionally locking out the compressor, or there is an electrical disconnect preventing the clutch from receiving power.

Next Troubleshooting Steps

To narrow down the exact cause of the lockout, you can move through these diagnostic checks:

  1. Test the Fuses and Relays: This is the most common and easiest issue to rule out. Locate the fuse box under the hood of your Malibu and check the owner's manual to identify the AC compressor clutch fuse and relay. If the fuse is intact, you can temporarily swap the AC relay with another identical relay in the box (such as the horn relay) to see if the compressor kicks on.
  2. Inspect the Compressor Wiring: Look closely at the electrical connector plugged directly into the side of the AC compressor. Ensure the clip is firmly seated and that the wires leading to it have not been frayed, melted, or damaged.
  3. Check the Clutch Coil Continuity: If the relays and wiring are fine, the electromagnet inside the compressor clutch may have failed. You can unplug the compressor connector and use a multimeter to check for continuity across the terminals. If there is infinite resistance (an open circuit), the clutch coil is dead and requires replacement.
  4. Evaluate the Pressure Transducer: Modern vehicles use a pressure sensor to tell the computer exactly how much pressure is in the system. If this sensor fails, it can send a faulty reading to the computer, prompting it to lock out the compressor as a safety measure to prevent damage.

Do not add any refrigerant from your recharge kit while troubleshooting these electrical and mechanical components. Pushing refrigerant into a dormant system will overcharge it, creating a secondary and potentially dangerous issue once the compressor is finally able to engage.

That is a fair assumption to make for now. If the fuse is completely intact, we can temporarily bypass the relay as the main suspect and work our way down the physical components of the system.

Since the compressor is definitively locked out, the vehicle's computer is either intentionally disabling it for safety, or the physical electromagnet inside the clutch has failed.

Here is the hierarchy of what to test next, starting with the easiest visual checks:

1. Visual Inspection of the Compressor Wiring

The compressor clutch relies on a direct electrical connection to engage.

  • The Check: Locate the actual AC compressor down by the serpentine belt. Look for the electrical wire harness plugging directly into the side or back of it.
  • What to Look For: Ensure the plug is firmly clicked into place. Inspect the wires leading up to it to make sure they haven't been chafed by the engine belt, melted by the exhaust, or chewed by rodents.

2. The Radiator Cooling Fans

The AC system relies on airflow across the condenser (mounted in front of the radiator) to remove heat.

  • The Check: Start the car and turn the AC to maximum cold. Walk around to the front of the car and look at the radiator fans.
  • What to Look For: If the fans are not spinning, the vehicle's computer will often intentionally lock out the AC compressor to prevent the engine from overheating and the AC system from over-pressurizing.

3. The A/C Pressure Sensor (Transducer)

This sensor tells the computer exactly what the pressure is inside the lines. If this sensor fails internally, it can default to telling the computer the system is completely empty or dangerously over-pressurized, causing an immediate compressor lockout.

  • The Check: This sensor is typically threaded directly into one of the aluminum AC lines (often the high-side liquid line).
  • What to Look For: Do a visual check of its wiring harness to ensure it is plugged in and undamaged. Diagnosing the sensor itself requires reading its live voltage output.

4. The Compressor Clutch Coil

If the computer is sending the signal to engage the compressor, but the electromagnet inside the pulley is dead, the center plate will never spin.

  • The Check: This requires unplugging the wire harness at the compressor and testing the two metal pins inside the compressor's connector.
  • What to Look For: You are looking for standard electrical resistance (usually between 3 to 5 ohms). If the reading is infinite, the internal coil wire is broken and the clutch is dead.

Do you happen to have a digital multimeter or an OBD2 diagnostic scanner on hand to test the electrical continuity or read the pressure sensor data?

turns.prompt_text: I have a digital multimeter so I can check the relay. 98124 continuity I see there are four prongs
turns.response_html:
That is perfect. Having a digital multimeter allows you to rule out the relay with a lot more certainty.

A standard 4-pin automotive relay acts as an electrically controlled switch. It contains two separate internal circuits:

  • The Coil Circuit (Control): Two of the prongs connect to an internal electromagnet coil. When the car's computer sends low-voltage power to these prongs, the coil magnetizes.
  • The Switch Circuit (Load): The other two prongs are the actual heavy-duty switch that sends power to the AC compressor. When the coil magnetizes, it pulls this switch closed.

Here is how to test both circuits using your multimeter.

Step 1: Identify the Prongs

Look at the bottom of the relay where the prongs are located, or look at the side of the plastic casing. You will often see numbers stamped next to the prongs or a small wiring diagram:

  • Pins 85 and 86: These are usually the Coil pins.
  • Pins 30 and 87: These are usually the Switch pins.
  • Note: If your relay lacks numbers, the coil pins are typically smaller or sit parallel to each other, while the switch pins might be slightly larger or perpendicular.

Step 2: Test the Coil for Resistance

This checks if the electromagnet inside the relay is intact or broken.

  1. Set your digital multimeter to the Ohms (Ω) setting to measure resistance.
  2. Touch one multimeter probe to Pin 85 and the other probe to Pin 86 (it does not matter which color probe goes to which pin).
  3. Read the screen:
    • A healthy relay coil will typically show a resistance reading anywhere between 50 and 120 Ohms.
    • If the multimeter reads OL (Open Line) or Infinite, the coil wire inside is snapped. The relay is completely dead and must be replaced.
    • If it reads 0 Ohms (or extremely close to 0), the coil is shorted out and the relay is dead.

Step 3: Test the Switch for Unpowered Continuity

This ensures the switch hasn't melted and fused itself together.

  1. Keep the multimeter on the Ohms (Ω) setting, or switch it to the Continuity setting (the icon that looks like sound waves, which beeps when a circuit is complete).
  2. Touch one probe to Pin 30 and the other to Pin 87.
  3. Read the screen:
    • Because the relay is currently unplugged and unpowered, the switch should be resting in the "open" (off) position.
    • Your multimeter should read OL (Open Line) and it should not beep.
    • If you get a reading near 0 Ohms or the multimeter beeps constantly, the switch is stuck in the closed position. The relay is broken and must be replaced.

The Limitation of the Unpowered Test

If your relay passes both Step 2 and Step 3, it is most likely fine.

However, to be 100% certain, you would need to perform a "bench test" with power. This involves using jumper wires to apply 12 volts directly from the car's battery to pins 85 and 86. You would hear an audible "click" as the coil activates, and you would then use your multimeter on pins 30 and 87 to verify that the resistance drops from OL to near 0 Ohms while the power is applied.

turns.prompt_text: So this is satisfying to me that it is working I do have an odb2 plugged into the vehicle. I could read data from that
turns.response_html:
That is excellent. Confirming the relay is healthy eliminates a major electrical variable, and having an OBD2 scanner that can read live data is exactly what you need to bridge the gap between the physical hardware and the vehicle's computer.

Since you know the physical static pressure in the lines is 87 psi, your goal now is to see what the vehicle's computer thinks the system state is. The computer relies on sensors to make the decision to engage the compressor, and if a sensor is lying, the system gets locked out.

Plug in your scanner, turn the vehicle's ignition to the "ON" position (engine running or just electronics on, but engine running is better to see if commands change), and navigate to the Live Data or Data Stream menu.

Look for the Engine Control Module (ECM) or Body Control Module (BCM) data stream, and search for these specific parameters:

1. A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor

This is the most critical piece of data. It might be labeled as A/C Press, Refrig Press, or A/C Sensor. It will display either in PSI or in Voltage (V).

  • What you want: The scanner's PSI reading should closely match the 87 psi you saw on your physical gauge. If it displays voltage, a normal resting static pressure usually reads somewhere around 1.0V to 1.5V.
  • The Red Flag: If the scanner reads 0 psi (or close to 0.0V), or if it reads maxed out at something like 400+ psi (or near 5.0V), your physical pressure transducer has failed. The computer is locking out the clutch because it thinks the system is either dangerously empty or about to explode.

2. A/C Request Signal

This parameter monitors the physical button inside the cabin. It will simply read ON or OFF (or YES/NO).

  • What you want: When you press the AC button on your dashboard, this should immediately toggle to ON.
  • The Red Flag: If it stays OFF no matter what you do, the climate control module on the dashboard isn't communicating with the main computer.

3. A/C Compressor Command (or A/C Relay Command)

This tells you what the computer is actually doing with the information it receives.

  • What you want: If the system is healthy, this should read ON, meaning the computer is actively trying to send power to the relay you just tested.
  • The Red Flag: If this reads OFF while the A/C Request reads ON, the computer is intentionally denying the compressor command due to a lockout condition (like a bad pressure sensor reading, or high engine coolant temperature).

If the computer says it is commanding the compressor ON, but the clutch isn't spinning, then the issue lies in the wiring between the relay box and the compressor, or the compressor's internal coil is dead.

turns.response_html:
The diagnostic data in the file "Screenshot_20260726-053458.png" perfectly explains why the compressor clutch is stationary.

Code P0532-00: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor Circuit Low Voltage

This code confirms exactly why the vehicle's computer is locking out the compressor. The Engine Control Module (ECM) is receiving a low voltage reading from the pressure sensor, which the computer interprets as the system being entirely empty. Because the physical gauge on the recharge kit previously read 87 psi, the sensor is sending a false signal to the ECM.

Code U183A-00: Lost Communication with Telematics

This is a standard network communication code related to the vehicle's telematics system. It is entirely unrelated to the air conditioning system and can be disregarded for this troubleshooting process.

Next Steps for Repair

The discrepancy between the actual physical pressure in the lines and the data the ECM is receiving points directly to a failure at the sensor level.

  1. Inspect the Wiring: Locate the A/C pressure sensor, which is threaded into the aluminum high-side A/C line under the hood. Examine the electrical pigtail plugging into it. If the wires are chewed, frayed, or heavily corroded, repairing the wiring harness will restore the signal.
  2. Replace the Sensor: If the wiring is intact and the connector is firmly seated, the sensor itself has failed internally and must be replaced. The A/C pressure switch is mounted on a built-in Schrader valve. This valve seals the line when the sensor is unscrewed, so the A/C system does not need to be evacuated prior to removing the switch.

Bingo. You have successfully located the A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor connector.

The three wires are the absolute giveaway here. Unlike a simple 2-wire clutch or relay, a pressure transducer requires three circuits to function:

  1. 5-Volt Reference: Power supplied by the Engine Control Module (ECM).
  2. Ground: The return path to the ECM.
  3. Signal: The variable voltage sent back to the ECM that correlates to the pressure in the line.

Because your scanner is throwing a P0532-00 (Circuit Low Voltage) code, the ECM is seeing 0 volts on that signal wire. This means either the sensor has internally failed and isn't sending the voltage back, or the wiring harness leading to this plug is severed (possibly in that mangled, silver-taped bundle you saw earlier).

Since you have a digital multimeter on hand, you can definitively pinpoint the culprit right now in just a few minutes.

The 5-Volt Reference Test

This test will tell you immediately if the wiring is broken or if the sensor itself is dead.

  1. Unplug the Connector: Depress the grey locking tab and pull the connector off the sensor.
  2. Power the Vehicle: Turn your vehicle's ignition to the ON position so the dashboard lights up, but do not start the engine.
  3. Set the Multimeter: Set your multimeter to read DC Volts.
  4. Test the Pins:
    • Place your black multimeter probe on a solid, unpainted metal ground (a bolt on the engine block or the negative battery terminal).
